game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is engrossing and more than a bit disturbing considering the implications of some very real things that are happening in the world right now. More of an interactive novel than a proper game, it nonetheless pulled me in for the 3-4 hours it took to reach the end of it, as well as a couple of replays to try out different paths.

It's not perfect, though; there's no challenge in actually getting the information you require since it's highlighted for you and you simply have to upload it, which sort of takes most of the initiative out of your hands. You do get to decide how certain characters are viewed based on how much you pass on to the powers that be, and your choices affect how they're treated and what happens to them, but the prevailing narrative is more or less canned, on-rails, and you can't do very much to affect how it plays out other than within a narrow scope. Some of the decisions you make do have very profound consequences for the individuals concerned, and the first time through I did have a few things I deeply regretted because of what happened as a result.


The biggest downside is that the game is short and fairly linear; there are only so many branches/possibilties to explore, so once you've exhausted them, there's really not much replay value. 

I've seen a few comparisons made to Papers, Please, which is less slick to play but rather more profound to actually experience because of the huge number of variations in how it can go. Orwell comparatively lacks depth, but because you spend more time with all the characters and get to know them better (since you're snooping through their gadgets and availing yourself of some very personal details of their lives), what happens to them matters a lot more to you. At least, it mattered more to me. In Papers Please I was more concerned with getting myself and my family out of dodge. 

Think of Orwell as an interactive dystopian techno-thriller and you've got a pretty good idea what you're in for.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You (in short, Orwell) is a five-part episodic narrative-driven mystery video game by Osmotic Studios set in a dystopian world in which the player assumes the role of a governmental operative who monitors surveillance sources to discovery national security threats. The game is named after the famed anti-totalitarian writer George Orwell and is inspired by themes established by his magnum opus novel, 1984.

The story in Orwell takes place in a country named The Nation which is governed by a contemporary authoritarian government known as The Party. Due to a series of events in the past, The Party passed the Safety Bill which expanded the government's capability to spy on its citizens in the name of national security. To accomplish this, the Ministry of Security, at the helm of Secretary of Security Catherine Delacroix, built a secret surveillance system codenamed Orwell. After a successful application and being selected from a pool of candidates, the player takes the role of an outsourced Orwell investigator who lives outside The Nation and is tasked, with the help of an assigned advisor going by the alias of Symes, to find evidence on the terrorist (individual or group) who caused a bomb explosion during a presumably peaceful protest in the populated Freedom Plaza in Bonton, the capital city of The Nation, destroying a statue and killing several people. The player soon stumbles upon an activist group called Thought who advocates for freedom of speech with anti-governmental sentiments, yet unaware of Orwell, who is entangled in the bombing incident. From there on, the player uses everything at their disposal to find evidence to expectantly incriminate their first suspect, Cassandra Watergate, an artist who was present at the Plaza shortly before the explosion.

The story occurs across five days (episodes) and what originally seemed like another day at the office, turns into an intricate roller-coaster of a journey full of conspiracy theories, deception and shocking revelations. The narrative in Orwell is exceptionally well-written and what keeps the player on their toes and constantly engaged. Just as things might get slightly monotonous now and again, the story always seems to throw you a new bone through unexpected plot twists and interestingly branched out paths shaped by your various choices and consequences. Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer.

All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed.

One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead.

Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting.

In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels.

Stay vigilant.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]My playtime:[/b] 10h (based on steam, 100% achievement; 2.5x playthrough)
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (17 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a massive information gathering system where you, an investigator, is taking a role in sorting the relevant data and fix conflicting data that the system gathered to assist a crime. The game has story branching that persists over 5 chapters.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 5 chapters
- Multiple endings and story branching that persists over the chapters
- Clean and fresh-looking interface
- You can restart a chapter after you finished the game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Phone calls and chat animations take a very long time to finish
- Some clues are too hard to deduce unless if you know the full story
- You can't press the button to show conflicting data sometimes

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read or stalk people, you should buy this game. You also can buy it at a discount if you think that the playtime isn't worth the full price.[/i]

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The interface is clean and fresh-looking. I like how the summary that is shown at the end of the chapter is introduced; it looks like the workboard in my office except that it's way cleaner.

As someone who likes to try something by doing it firsthand, I don't find the design to be confusing. The portal section looks like your regular website, the message section looks like your regular chat app, and the device section looks like the simpler version of your device.

I'm also impressed by how the dev showed the photos; it looks like a fragmented version of our faces and it looks so detailed even though it's not. The important facial like eyes and hair is shown although most details are blurred and fragmented.

The cutscene at the prologue skipped a few frames to me though, although I don't have any trouble in understanding the story because of that.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is being told by several conversations of your "adviser", someone who deduce things based on your findings, and whatever you read when you try to find clues, which are mostly from chat and phone calls.

Even though most conversations are held this way, I didn't find the main story to be confusing. Even if you couldn't understand the story, the "adviser" will give you some sort of info as to what is happening so you should be fine as long as you don't skip it. There's also a summary at the end of the chapter if you want to keep track of things.

There are several branchings in the game, either minor or major. I find the conversation between the branches to be smooth although some parts confused me since I didn't know the whole story at that moment. You need to play several playthroughs throughout the game to get all the major story branches and understand the whole story.

The thing is, there is no good or bad ending in this game; it's all about your opinion. You think what you think is good and bad. You also can deduce the whole story if you want or you can just understand the main story and be done with it.

[h1]The game[/h1]
[b]Features[/b]
There are 3 sections where you do most of your work: portal, message, and device. The in-game name is different, but I can't seem to recall the actual name since you don't need to know about the name to use it.

The portal consists of several web pages that you can access. The pages that you can access are limited to the system and more will show up as you unlock more clues.

The message, on the other hand, is a bit different. A message, either chat, email, or phone, will show up at certain times and you're allowed to wire-tap their chat and calls in real-time. The thing is, the chat speed is very slow. You can speed up the phone chat speed a bit although I still want it to be faster. It's taking too much time to listen to it especially when you're replaying your playthrough.

The device can be activated after you obtain a serial number of the target's device. You can access all files in the device, whether it's from a desktop or phone.

[b]Investigation[/b]
The suspect will have a profile page that you can fill with data. These data can be obtained by browsing through the 3 sections I mentioned. The data that you can take will be highlighted, either in blue or yellow.

Blue-colored means that there is no conflict with the data and yellow means that the data contradicts with other data. The game also has an option to show the conflicting data although I find that it's not working sometimes.

The thing is, you have freedom in choosing whatever you submit. I thought that I should fill all of the highlighted data in blue for complete profiling, but it's actually the opposite. All the data that you fill will be useful for the advisor's judgment and other people's fate, so you should decide carefully on what you submit.

Some data that you submit will change the story greatly, some are not. However, there are times where you have to make a major guess in determining the conflicting data that you must submit because you didn't know much and the clues are too vague at that point. Luckily, as I said before, there are no good and bad endings, so you can proceed as you please.

[b]Replayability and Length[/b]
As I said before, there are multiple endings. There are 5 chapters in total and each chapter except the last one lasts around 1 hour. I played the game fully twice and played one last playthrough from chapter 3 to unlock all of the major branching and achievement. It took me around 4 hours to finish all chapters at once.

Each chapter has a minimum of 2 endings that will affect the subsequent chapter. You can restart the whole story from the beginning or replay the chapter if you want after you finish the game once. Restarting the game from a specific chapter will delete all of the subsequent chapter data though.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
It's a nice game where you have to browse through things and wiretap people's communication to find out whatever is going on. The game has a lot of story branching and replayability.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]The book 1984 by author George Orwell in a game. Splendid and intresting. While I've only read half of the book, I can still understand the connections. This must not happen in real life. I know it already does.. But we can still stop it..[/h1]
Ýou're yourself, a investigator with amazing spying tools. You get to spy on timelines, emails and even wire-tap phones.
You are looking for connections to put terrorists behind bars. The terrorists are bombing several buildings in Bonton, a fictional city in The Nation, a country where a Safety Bill has just gone through that puts investigators into control of the police work of The Nation. As a investigator for the law enforcement it is up to you to put the terrorists behind bars using Orwell. Orwell is a tool developed to find perpetrators before the crime is done. While there is flaws, terrorists and their groups are linked way faster than a human would think without the help of computers and social media sniffing.

[h1]This should remind us all of how NSA, FRA and GCHQ spies on us all today. No matter where we live in this damned world.[/h1]
Orwell is a scary game.. You never know what your state knows about you.. In some countries, people with odd political beliefs are put behind bars, freethinkers are disappearing and people who voted wrong are found and assaulted in their homes. While Orwell did not cover any of these points, it still covered the great amount of Internet hate you can get if you do anything wrong, even if it is just a single thing.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]

[list]
    [*]60+ FPS during the whole playthrough.
    [*]Think you're a NSA spy.
    [*]Very intresting.
[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]

[list]
    [*]The game is far too short. I wanted to play more when I was to be arrested for knowing too much about Orwell..
    [*]It was buggy at times where I couldn't upload data until I restarted the game.
    [*]Nothing else.
[/list]

[h1]Ending notes of this quick review[/h1]
I am recommending this game to anyone, no matter age. This is a good game to learn from. Learn how the regime works. Learn how your country works. No matter if you live in a democracy or not there is always gonna be Big Brother spying on you. This game is more than just a simple game that only a fraction of people will buy. This game is a lifelesson worth getting. Nobody really cares how innocent you are. You are always a suspect when it comes  to state business.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Orwell is a fresh new take on the visual novel game format. The game UI immediately immerses the player, placing you squarely in the driver seat as you try to unravel a bombing plot and pursue justice... but for whom?[/h1]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
You take on the role of a government surveillance cyber-investigator. Your task is to get into a person’s life through their social media, bank accounts, phone taps and chat messages. Drag and drop important bits of information (data chunks) into the ORWELL interface to upload these bits of data to form dossiers and help your supervisor inform the local authorities. 

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Evocative Experience[/u][/b]: 
Almost immediately, you’ll be oriented into the role of a cyber surveillance investigator and the stakes don’t get much higher than trying to unravel a terrorist plot. This game will make you *[b]feel[/b]* things and think about morality. 

[*][b][u]Novel UI [/u][/b]:
I think the UI is definitely the best part of the game, as it is designed in such a way to evoke the feeling of using some official piece of government software. Most of your interactions are in the form transcribed phone conversations, chat logs and browsing “online” content. 

[*][b][u]Art Style[/u][/b]:
The pixelated, somewhat-cartoony photos of people and places creates the perfect balance of reality and surreality. Probably for the best, as the game’s primary focus is to get you thinking about the heavy moral issues related to a surveillance society, as depicted by the game’s very Orwellian world. 

[*][b][u]Music[/u][/b]: Almost invisible, but ever present, the music stylings accented the drama perfectly. 
[/list]

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Lack of Visual Information[/u][/b]: 
A significant part of this game is reading text. Which you then choose to upload to Orwell or ignore (depending on the context of the circumstances and your personal value system).  

However, there were several times when I literally could not continue the game because the next event had to be triggered by me uploading some [b][u]some very specific, but unknown[/u][/b] piece of data. This created a situation where I would upload more info than I wanted to, just in an effort to trigger the next cutscene. 

Rather than guessing, it would have been nice if the designers could have implemented a color system or some other way to indicate what data was tied to progressing the story. I suppose the current implementation is more true to life, but it lessened my sense of agency when I would upload some seemingly innocuous data and suddenly my supervisor would dm me with a new break in the case. 

[*][b][u]File Organization[/u][/b]: 
By the end of the game, there are dozens of pages of fictitious files and documents to sift through... and the game did NOT make that task much easier. Could I get some bookmarks, please?

[*][b][u]RAILROADING[/u][/b]: 
So, I won’t say much here out of respect for spoilers, but suffice it to say that the design choices made in the game make it very clear how the developers feel regarding the subject matter. This bias in design limited the scope of user choice and the kinds of endings you can get. It would have been very interesting to have a greater variety of outcomes. It would have also worked to underscore the sense of user agency that they’d worked so hard to create in the first place.

[*][b][u]Short Length [/u][/b]: 
I’ve finished 2 complete playthroughs at 11 hours... which, given the minimalism of the graphics, seems extremely short and makes the current price of $9.99 a bit pricey.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Overall a very interesting and unique experience that I mostly enjoyed. However, because of the political nature of the game and the railroading embedded by the developers, I don’t think I’ll be buying any DLC any time soon, nor would I recommend the game at its current price of $9.99.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] How far are you willing to go to protect the populace? [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is a “visual novel” style game in which you have the ability to follow cyber-breadcrumbs in order to slowly uncover suspect’s online lives. Your goal? Stop a terrorist organization (?) from bombing public spaces. Your tools? As an agent, you are privy to the entirety of your target’s posts, articles, phone calls, emails, etc. Use this information to reveal more and more relevant webpages and conversations. The catch? You’re overlooked by a supervisor and you must choose what information to upload. This supervisor can only see the bits of information you feed him, so choose wisely or risk ruining an innocent’s life. The challenge? Upload only enough information to gain new leads, but not jump to conclusions. 

Are you really helping the greater good by invading the privacy of the few? Or have you caused more harm than good, muddling in affairs you should have never been in? Are the internet spies of today, really the superheroes of tomorrow? Find out by stepping into these large, cyber shoes. Act quickly and stop a harmful event in its tracks, or wait it out and discover it was a false alarm. Big brother is watching you. You are watching the people. Lives are on the line. Decide. 

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b]

Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far.

[h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. 

[b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later.

[b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?) 

[b]Intriguing artwork.[/b] The geometric artistic style lends itself to unconsciously nod its head towards the cyber-oriented world of the game. It ties in beautifully to the theme of the game—from the logo to the interface—without being too aggressive.

[h1]Cons:[/h1] [strike][b]A better save system!![/b][/strike] Update has added a rewind system, but I have not played since [strike]I cannot stress this enough. Since this is a consequence-based game, I’d like to be able to start from the end episode one, or so, with my decisions staying the same, and only make changes to my decisions from there out, with my profiles branching out from my first play through plot line. Starting over from the beginning is too much of a grind. Even a way to speed up messaging/call text on the second (and beyond) playthrough would be better for acheivement hunters or people just curious about the other endings. Examples of games with a good save system for this style of gameplay include [i]A Wolf Among Us[/i] and [i]Papers, Please.[/i][/strike]

[b]A bit linear, limited.[/b] There were some moments I wish some bit of text was highlighted (you may only drag and upload highlighted data chunks) since I wanted to explore that avenue of inquiry, but [i]Orwell[/i] had other plans. This gave the game a restricted feeling. It does not leave the game open to a world of naturally-occurring red herrings (only game-constructed ones, not user constructed), which I think would have added much more depth to the game. Also, it’s glaringly obvious which pieces of text carry great significance. (Those will be the ones with conflicting evidence) so sometimes the challenge of deciding to report information right away or wait was quite discernible, offering no challenge. Although, I will say that there are a few nuggets of data I uploaded without believing they would have as large of a consequence as they did. 

[b]Short.[/b] There’s only a little over forty minutes of game play per episode, and with five episodes, this leads to roughly four hours of gameplay (assuming you don’t replay events). I follow a rule of thumb of at least $1 to 1 hour of gameplay, so in that regard, it’s a bit pricey. Just wait for a sale. 

[h1]Remark:[/h1] [b]Play in one sitting[/b] (or as close to that as possible, if you don't have a full 4-5 hours to dedicate to one game) The flow and length of the game lends itself to be optimally played in one sitting. Taking a break and not have a comprehensive refresher (like the cinematic playbacks of key choices in [i]Telltale[/i] games) of your choices and actions is jarring to the enjoyment of the storyline in my opinion.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
[b]I’d recommend buying [i]Orwell[/i] when on sale.[/b] It has an interesting and captivating storyline, despite some need of polishing. The interface, flow, and artwork lend itself to be an immersive experience into the lives of the people you are spying on to protect. Also, the current social commentary gives a real-world depth to the game. It does feel a bit restricting at times, and the story is short. The save system leaves much to be desired, since I would like to more easily explore all possibilities of my choices. But, despite these factors it was still enjoyable and fun to play.

Although, I will say that there are a few nuggets of data I uploaded without believing they would have as large of a consequence as they did. [b]Short.[/b] There’s only a little over forty minutes of game play per episode, and with five episodes, this leads to roughly four hours of gameplay (assuming you don’t replay events). I follow a rule of thumb of at least $1 to 1 hour of gameplay, so in that regard, it’s a bit pricey. Just wait for a sale. [h1]Remark:[/h1] [b]Play in one sitting[/b] (or as close to that as possible, if you don't have a full 4-5 hours to dedicate to one game) The flow and length of the game lends itself to be optimally played in one sitting. Taking a break and not have a comprehensive refresher (like the cinematic playbacks of key choices in [i]Telltale[/i] games) of your choices and actions is jarring to the enjoyment of the storyline in my opinion. [h1]Conclusion:[/h1] [b]I’d recommend buying [i]Orwell[/i] when on sale.[/b] It has an interesting and captivating storyline, despite some need of polishing. The interface, flow, and artwork lend itself to be an immersive experience into the lives of the people you are spying on to protect. Also, the current social commentary gives a real-world depth to the game. It does feel a bit restricting at times, and the story is short. The save system leaves much to be desired, since I would like to more easily explore all possibilities of my choices. But, despite these factors it was still enjoyable and fun to play.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I have been playing video games since the Atari 2600 and out of the many games I have played only 5  have inspired me to award them my own personal score of 10. Orwell has joined this very exclusive list for me. The game is a masterclass of using the medium of video games to make poignant social commentary that feels gripping and authentic. 

Daniel Marx (Game Designer) is a fantastic writer who gives each one of his characters a very distinct voice using colloquial dialogue and expressions that stay consistent for each character throughout the course of the 5 chapters of the story. His ability to create believable characters with personalities and motivations that feel real is the key to making the message of the game resonate. This isn't a simple story of noble heroes and evil villains, this is an examination of complex people and their struggles to reconcile their beliefs and their feelings, their fears and their ability to summon up the courage to do what they feel is right. 

The Gameplay is simple to understand, but choices made by the player do have branching consequences. Reminiscent of Telltale games and other members of the narrrative genre with a choice driven structure. The game manages to give the player a sense of real agency in the outcomes of the story, and have genuinley significant differences at several key moments. My mind spins at the challenge of writing a story that is able to stay consistent throughout its length, and yet offer a significant number of alternatives that need to be followed to their logical conclusion. Again, my compliments to Daniel Marx on his writing skills and game design. Impressive. Very impressive. 

The art style reminded me of the polygonal look of games like Out of This World and Flashback from the early and mid 90's with improved technology that looks good and yet remains accessible to all players even ones with 8 year old laptops (such as myself). Compliments to Melanie Taylor for an aesthetic that is easy on the eye and hardware. 

In the end, the writing, gameplay and art all serve to execute on making a statement about the ever increasing surveillance that is taking place in our own world and it is no suprise that the invasion of privacy that is possible at this very moment is something that can chill to the bone. We are at a crossroads in the story of humanity, whether the next chapters are dominated by the decision to sacrifice freedom for security or the acceptance that freedom carries risks, but is far better than a world where everyone is always suspect of being an enemy of the state and a target for elimination. 

Provided you do not object to reading a great deal (as there is no voice acting), this game will provide you with 10 hours of riveting narrative that will undoubtedly leave you questioning how much autonomy we are willing to surrender for the illusion of safety that a large surveillance state seemingly affords. 

I cannot recommend this game highly enough.

P.S. Additionally many thanks to Michael Kluge (Programming) for his coding work. The game runs very well. Amazing that this trio of developers crafted such a landmark title. I bow to your triumvirate of talent. 

P.P.S : Incidentally, in case anyone is interested, my other Perfect 10 games are :

- Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time
- Resident Evil 4
- Batman : Arkham City
- Last of Us
- Telltale's The Walking Dead : Season 1

Very different from Orwell, but masterpieces for me in the revolution in video game design they brought to different elements of the industry.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A poignant game on the times we live in. I'm a humongous fan of the "Walking Simulator" genre and I stumbled upon this game during the Steam Winter Sale (3 days ago). Orwell has a captivating storyline that takes the "first person" experience quite literally. Without spoiling the game, the story focuses on a user operated software called Orwell, where the player assumes the role as a operator outside the fictatious "Nation", spying on activists that are tagged as potentially violent. 

The user interface is streamlined, dare I say "user-friendly". The fictional profiles depicted in the video game are unnervingly real, pulling me into the experience, as though as I really am spying on others. The characters are well scripted, albeit being scripts of text. The characters are caricatures of stereotypical activists, with complex backgrounds and hidden agendas. 

The "orwellian" connotations that are hinted at in the game are subtle, nuanced without being too overbearing or obvious. As you progressively submit information on labelled targets, you start to feel a heavy burden of responsibility on your shoulders. The multiple options and consequences from submitting false information add more weight to the situation. The activities or rituals performed by the main character are a frighteningly realistic, depecting the state of the world we live in. 

My only complaints include the duration of the game: it is rather short in length, more like a concept game showcasing some of the developer's strengths. The waiting times between each mission is abysmal, sometimes resulting in multiple crashes. 

All in all, this is an underrated gem in the walking simulator category, standing tall with the likes of Gone Home and Soma.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a game that I have mixed feeling about. While I did enjoy the game, I also want to clarify that there is certainly more than one issue with the game that makes me want to not recommend it.

The gameplay boils down to one and only one mechanic. Being able to drag selected text into a profile which affects the story. You need to bounce between internet pages, phone-call logs, and a few other forms of data to find keywords and important text to upload. Depending on what you upload, what the government believes and what happens to the person(s) involved changes. Do you portray a spoiled brat as a terrorist? An old man as a kind teacher. You decide what information they've put online defines them, very literally. 

The issues I have with this is as such: 
[olist]
    [*]Choices don't ultimately matter.
    [*]It is painfully short.
    [*]A lack of any audio design.
[/olist]

From top to bottom, the linearity of the game. Despite being able to chose what information does or doesn't get uploaded, a lot (and I do mean a LOT) of events will happen regardless of your actions. The game literally says in it's description: "But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences." However, despite this, the only things my choices ended up affecting were the achievements. And spoiler alert: [spoiler] You can get any of the three endings no matter what choices you made in previous episodes. [/spoiler] Sure, on a superficial surface level your choices have consequences, but these "consequences" never actually impact your story or gameplay expericence.

Onto the next, the length. You may see me having 7.5 hours and tell me "Oh well 7.5 hours in NOT a short game!" You'd be right. Except Orwell is not 7.5 hours long, it is 3 hours long at most and 2 hours long at it's shortest. The only reason I have more than 3 hours of playtime is because I went back to get all of the achievements, which is also why i know how little your choices affect the story. I've seen all the endings, seen the affect of almost all of the choices, and even then with some time spent idle I was able to see 99% of this game's offerings in under 8 hours. This isn't inherently bad, but Orwell has little to no gameplay, audio design, or anything. It's just an on rails story, and for it to be that short for a $10 USD price tag is a little much.

Lastly, the audio design. As previously mentioned, there is little to no audio in this game. You have 3 music tracks, the main menu theme, the basic ambient theme and a more intense theme for when things "get serious." Outside of the music, you might have a few computer beeps or a quick musical tone at random points, but they're so spread out that a majority of your time is spent with almost nothing going into your ears. You can't hear people on their phone calls, your boss can't speak to you, there are no audio transcripts. It is the most barebones audio design I've seen in a story driven game.

The only really good thing I'd argue in favor of is the art style. It is a fractal/cubism artstyle that absolutely draws you in. The issue is that this art style is not the primary focus, instead that focus is on a painfully bland UI. If you look at the screenshots on the store page, you see that profile tab on the right, your bar up top and the righthand screen? That is 90% of the game. Just looking at those screens It could've been so much more.

I really like the idea of Orwell, an Orwellian (pun not intended) dystopia with a spying government and terrorist plots. The thing that makes me not like it though is literally everything else about it. And that is the problem.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h3][i]“War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]


Even if you haven't read anything by George Orwell, you've probably heard about 1984. The dystopia the author foresaw has undoubtedly materialized in the modern world, as most readers of the book like to point out. This assertion is without doubt true; even if you only use the internet for personal purposes, there are still a lot of data crumbs left behind. You can never be certain if someone is keeping an eye on your every online move, whether it be a post about a recent vacation, a comment made on a forum, or the address you use to sign emails. 
This is precisely what Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You promises: it is a game about a reality that nobody wants to face but that hangs in the air.

[h3][i]“The consequences of every act are included in the act itself.”[/i] - George Orwell[/h3]

The game takes place in the capital of a fictional country called The Nation, where on April 12th, 2017, a terrorist attack occurs: a bomb detonates in the famous Freedom Plaza, destroying a statue and killing several people. At the same time, the police receive a note containing the first three stanzas of a German folk song called The Thoughts are Free.

In 2012, The Party, a paternalistic government that leads The Nation, passed the Safety Bill, which gave the government complete freedom over citizens' personal data and the ability to spy on them using a surveillance system called Orwell. This is where your involvement with The Nation begins.
You are the first person who has been selected to be an investigator - a citizen outside of The Nation, who will use Orwell to uncover as much data about a person as possible. You are being accompanied by an Advisor, who will connect you to the authorities. 

The plot is essentially a classic detective whodunit story told in five chapters; throughout the game, multiple suspects will emerge, and your job will be to determine each person's involvement and, in the end, find the perpetrator(s) - or is it?
The aforementioned data (which the game refers to as datachucks) gathering is the game's main essence and gameplay mechanic - you have access to a wide range of websites, phones, e-mail addresses, and even computers, where you must find information related to your lead. This isn't a difficult task because the game highlights them in blue or yellow; the latter indicates a data collision, and you must determine which is the correct data.

A few things should be kept in mind with this mechanic: first, it is completely irreversible - once you upload something in the system, there is no way to change it, and the story will proceed accordingly; second, you do not need to upload every possible datachunk - at first, the game forces you to do this, but later you must be careful what you upload; and third, the game is actually a choose-your-own-adventure with a detective façade - given that there are multiple endings, your choices will have a heavy impact on the story.

Orwell's strength is the moral uncertainty it contains. Players will have to weigh the pros and cons of sharing new information with the people they're investigating versus keeping it to themselves as they gather additional evidence. Because of this, players will feel more invested in the game and more emotionally connected to their choices.

[h3][i]“But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]

One of the game's greatest strengths is its immersive and atmospheric presentation. The dark and minimalist art style, combined with a haunting original soundtrack, sets the perfect tone for an oppressive world governed by The Party. The user interface is sleek and intuitive, allowing easy navigation of the vast amount of information at your disposal. Towards the end of the game, the interface will get much more crowded; however, the game displays a red icon next to a document where new data chunks can be found. Furthermore, the game's soundtrack perfectly complements the dystopian atmosphere, with haunting melodies and industrial beats that immerse players in the world of surveillance and control. 

Orwell does, however, have a few minor flaws. As the investigation progresses through a series of data-mining tasks, the gameplay can feel slow at times. Some players, particularly those who prefer more action-oriented experiences, may find these moments tedious. Furthermore, while the game encourages players to take different paths, the overall impact of your choices on the narrative can feel somewhat limited, leaving some room for a more dynamic and personalized experience unexplored.
The length of the game is another aspect of the experience that could be improved. The story is interesting and the decisions are weighty, yet the game is over in a matter of hours and it left me craving for more. The game's depth of topic and potential for replay may have benefited from more content or branching routes.



[h3][i]“Freedom is the freedom to say that two plus two make four. If that is granted, all else follows.”[/i]
 - George Orwell[/h3]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a fascinating and unsettling adventure that delves into the moral issues raised by omniscient monitoring and the misuse of authority. A standout in the narrative-driven genre, thanks to its engaging tale, accessible gameplay, and morally weighty choices. Even though it's not particularly long and has a few weaker points, it's a must-play if you enjoy engaging stories set in dystopian futures.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
OK - to start with the bad; the way progression works is, to say the least, not exactly flawless. At multiple times I felt I had no choice but to do the exact opposite of what my intuition really led me towards, because if the story hasn't moved forward in a while, and you've already done everything that seems sensible, you've no real choice but to just take random stabs. You never know what will push the game to move the story forward, and unfortunately it can really weaken the immersion when you're going back to accept data points you had previously ruled out just on the off chance one of them will finally trigger the script to move forward.

Also, it sometimes feels a little restrictive that you are never freely choosing what information to select for processing - rather, you are selecting which of the automatically flagged information to process. So, sometimes it simply doesn't highlight something which might seem important to you, and sometimes the conclusions drawn from the information flagged isn't quite what you expected. To some extent, these can be forgiven as contributing to the theme that you are not entirely in control of the "Orwell" program, but nonetheless, this can also pull you out of the game if something really catches your attention but the lack of a flag is effectively the game telling you to ignore it.

Those minor irks aside, though - I actually thought this game was very good.

The story is interesting, and generally does an excellent job of avoiding lazy narrative tropes or character stereotypes. The combination of inferring information from investigating documents and reading call or chat transcripts as a means of piecing together events is used to excellent effect. Overall, the story is easily engaging enough to keep you invested in the game throughout, wanting to untangle all the details. 

The mechanics, despite the little irks I mentioned at the beginning of the review, also work really nicely on the whole. They feel genuinely fresh and original, and effectively encourage you to keep paying attention while working through a fairly hefty pile of documents.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Prelude:	[/h1]
For too long Telltale have had a vice grip on linear story-based games. Which is a shame considering only about 2 of their games were decent. So when I heard a new game had created enough favorable reviews and praise from people I trust, I decided to boot up: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, or rather, Orwell: generic subtitle. 

[h1] Gameplay:	[/h1]
The game consists of reading through text, selecting infomation to upload to Orwell, a huge data base supposedly allowing to keep endless amounts of infomation on people (more on this later) you select outlined text or images, and choose wether or not to upload the data. Most of the infomation is required, but the game does a fairly decent job of shaking things up, infomation conflicting and choosing which one is most significant, the worst choice being: An online commenter calls guy A 'homosexual' meanwhile in a newspaper, it is stated he has been happily married with children. You choose which source is reliable. There also ends up being a data mechanic, only alloweed to upload 20 data chunks. The game does a [u] really [/u] good job of rewarding the player to go further, for instance near the end of the second chapter ([b] SPOILERS [/b]): [spoiler] There is a bomb detonating soon, with two people potentially offering locations of the bomb, if you dig deep into the email or messages (I think) of the people, you can see him admitting that he let his idea be pushed down, then using dates and timestamps, you can figure out this was just after the two people offered the locations. 	[/spoiler] This not only makes the player feel great after solving this puzzle, but also affects the endgame too. However the endgame is EASILY the weakest part of the game.

It is the [u] exact [/u] game issue as telltale games, maybe even worse. On the nose the character's tell you what you did, so averty it feels stupid. Not to mention.. [spoiler] The secret ending is locked off depending on how you handled a situation in Chapter 3, where you have to actively fail at your job to reach the good ending telling the police that a woman is armed and has knowledge of military which is FACT, you have to actively NOT tell the police this info, and THEN tell them her correct location, despite the fact the character says: 'I am not going down without a fight.' And you can accidentally trigger endings randomly, with supposedly 3/4 choices layed down right at the end, then wanting to do extra research, it doesn't say 'Are you sure, this will end?' Or something like that.	[/spoiler]

[h1] Graphics:	[/h1]
These devs are smart, at least in this department. The game is extremely stylised, meaning it will age very well. There was one time where I wasn't sure who was in a picture due to this, and it came as a suprise to me. Otherwise a few issues, there is no voice acting, even on phone calls. This shouldn't be an issue, considering other MAJOR review sites can get away with subtracting points from a game for having good voice acting rather than nothing. (yeah im still angry) If you also have Dyslexia maybe give this one a miss, it is a LOT of reading, and if you dislike the font, it doesn't change often enough to merit trying with this one.

[h1] Other:	[/h1]
The soundtrack starts off great, being the perfect sort of tracks for reading, not distracting enough to take you out of the game, but enough to stand on it's own. There is a few 'sting tracks' where they are used for shock, and this works mostly, apart from near the end where you are simply scrolling down and then you see some text and DUNNN, which was suprising and took the shock out of what I was reading because I didn't have to read it in time. It also starts getting REALLY repetitive near the end.

The game REALLY tries to be replayable, with the ability to skip to chapters 1-5, but a big problem are the phone calls, they average around 4.5 minuites in real time. With the final one, Chapter 5, where you would WANT to go through again first, too see if it could have ended different lasts around 10 minuites, of non-interactable text, which you would have read already. The game also isn't too long, if you read every article and looked indepth for everything I can imagine it lasting at around 5 hours, if you skip text and just look at the highlighted text, around 3 hours. For me, my playthrough was around 4.7 hours. A decent time, not too long, not too short.

[h1] TL:DR:	[/h1]
If you enjoy linear story-based games and want to see a good attempt or just a LINEAR STORY GAME WITHOUT TELLTALE IN IT, and enjoy reading, then its a recommendation, if you don't fit all 3 of those criteria, wait until a Steam Sale, or a Humble Bundle like I did. It does hint at some cool political ideas and ideologies, but that's more in the sequal.

Nevertheless, I look forward for the next Orwell game to go on sale and be fully out, I am a cautious fan, please keep up the good work devs, nice to see some varation in the gaming scene. You seem like cool guys too, patching stuff in and so forth.

-Thanks for reading
-Cain

review_text_raw:
[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]A great and very frightening concept
[*]Awesome story
[*]Great replayabililty
[*]The design is just beautiful
[/list]


[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]First chapters get a bit stale after one or two playthroughs
[*]No way to speed up dialogue you’ve already read and just need to grab info from
[/list]

[h1]Review:[/h1]
The most terrifying part of Orwell is just how easily its events could come to pass in our own world. George Orwell himself could not have predicted the level of surveillance we all voluntarily subject ourselves to by keeping always-listening, always-tracking smart devices on our persons, in our cars, and in our homes. It doesn’t take a lot of imagination to see a system such as the one portrayed in the game being used by a real nation, especially since we know the United States already conducts mass surveillance in a multitude of ways.


Orwell (the game) did an excellent job keeping me on the edge of my seat throughout its entire duration. Even though you only interact with them (or rather, their information) through a screen, it was hard not to feel connected to the characters. Whether that connection is based on sympathy or a desire to lock them up is up to you.


The game lends itself well to multiple playthroughs in order to achieve different endings, and there are tons of different ways to get to those endings. However, by the second or third time the first few chapters begin to feel very repetitive. I often found myself checking my phone while waiting for in-game conversations to finish so I could decide which chunks of data to grab. There is tons of interesting stuff to read in Orwell, but it would be nice to skip past some dialogue when I’ve already read it three times.


The length of the game really surprised me. For $11 I didn’t expect as much story and detail as I got. While it only took me about 6 hours my first time through, and I can definitely go through quicker now if I wanted, looking over all of the great little details that have been thrown in definitely takes time. That’s not a bad thing, as Orwell’s realism is only helped by how believable its characters (and their social media profiles, emails, and phone calls) are.


This is definitely a great game, and it was an awesome surprise when I discovered it while browsing the web one day. Be warned, though - after you play you’ll often find yourself thinking about your online conversations, and if something you said years ago (or even yesterday) could somehow be used to incriminate you.

review_text_raw:
Lot of good, but outweighed by the bad.

The game was entertaining and built on a thought-provoking premise, but the game is far too short (roughly four hours in length) and the premise of the game loses its edge when the game picks a side on the question if society should sacrifice privacy for security instead of leaving that decision up to the player.

The story is well-written but offers very little in replayability. The games premise would have room for several scenarios where the player has to puzzle together what has happened or attempt to prevent crimes from happening, placing the player in situations where he has to weigh his decision how deep into someones private-life he should go to discover the truth, and even then be left with an uncertainty that forces him to make decisions based only his own interpretation of the truth. Instead, the game presents one scenario that plays out over a five-day period. The game-mechanics themselves are not complicated and the games graphics and presentation is mostly text and still-pictures, so more scenarios should not be difficult or time-consuming to add later on.

If the game had more meat on the bones I would recommend it, but for the moment this is a brief game with little replayability, but potential for a lot more.

review_text_raw:
Short and sweet.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is an interactive dystopian mystery clicker with one of the most obvious titles on this planet. Seriously, tell me you don't have an inkling of what this game is about just by reading it. No? 
Well - Orwell touches on government surveillance, privacy in the age of send/receive, newsfeeds and - on the philosophical level - shockingly personal themes such as morality, autonomy and group culture. It also teeters on the sociological side of things with themes of the looking-glass self, or how we present ourselves to the world/others. Let's talk about the narrative. I'll try not to spoil too much.

------------------------------------

You are, well, yourself. You live in a non-disclosed location as an investigator who has just been contracted to work on a secret government project by The Nation; A country that is, simply put, not doing so great from the leadership aspect. The Nation is undergoing political turmoil, both inner and outer, and is seeing a concerning increase in violence, extremism and terrorist attacks. This has led the country to establish increasingly dystopian methods of surveillance. 

The beginning scene sets the tone with you looking through multiple sets of cameras on an otherwise normal day in a city square. The cameras scan the citizens, seemingly referencing police files to determine if they're a threat. So far, so good! A blue haired girl quietly walks past and the camera begins to buzz, showing that - !!! - she has had an encounter with the law in the past. We tensely follow her as she gets on a bus and it drives away. Hm. Well, surely that's not THAT out of the ordinary, right? We all know someone who has a blot on their record. Surely, we shouldn't judge unless they've done something terrible? I'll reserve my judgement. 

And then a statue a short distance away is engulfed in dust, shrapnel and the sounds of an otherwise normal day being eviscerated as a bomb explodes. Well, damn.

This is where you come in, Investigator. You have been hired to test the efficacy of the brand new "Orwell" project. Orwell is a hot-off-the-assembly-line database tool that allows you to search nearly anything there is to know about a person. It creates links between people for referencing and logs any interesting findings you catch - referred to as 'datachunks' within each person's "file". Your job is to prevent any other terrorist attacks from occurring as well as finding out who could've been behind such a horrible event.

-------------------------------------

The success of Orwell is predicated on it's atmosphere - and it is indeed the game's biggest asset. However...

If I can be quite honest - the writing itself isn't anything revolutionary here when it comes to it's subject matter. Some of the dialogue is great, engrossing even. Some of it is extraordinarily cringey, for lack of a better word. A certain aforementioned blue-haired character comes to mind, especially near the end game. Some laughably unbelievable behavior occurs that can really mess with your vibe once you understand exactly how the plot is shaping itself.

Writing quibbles aside, immersion is ultimately what reigns supreme here. The developers have created such an oppressively paranoid atmosphere with the simple interface and nerve-wracking audio cues that it's incredibly easy to be charmed and overlook it's relatively short length. This is a game that benefits from not overstepping it's own ambition. 

I've seen a few other reviews being slightly critical of the fact that more characters weren't involved in the overall game - but I think that this actually works in Orwell's favor. The gameplay is the *absolute* definition of repetitive. You shift between tabs, you drag and you drop. That's it. If the gameplay wasn't so story centric and was more sim-based (with more options within the Orwell interface), I would agree with those criticisms and want to be Big Brother until the end of time. However, this is an actual story game. Consider this to be a dystopian choose your own adventure.

To end this ramble, let's talk length and price. I spent 3.4 hours on this game and completed it. It's currently $9.99 on Steam. I myself, being transparent, did not pay $9.99 for this. I received it in a bundle along with it's sequel. So you ultimately will have to make your own call here - but I will say that YES - Orwell is indeed worth $10 just for the first playthrough alone. 

Not very many games touch upon these themes, and I do consider these to be important themes considering the time/political climate we live in right now. Regardless of how successful the game is at making a statement on these themes, I appreciate the effort. And a lot of effort has gone into this game. 

I very much recommend you give it the chance, it may very well cause you to look over both digital shoulders.

review_text_raw:
Spying on citizens of a (not-so) future dystopian society in an attempt to convict them of crimes and uncover some deeper conspiracy sounds good on paper, but does not work so well in game form; at least not if it is done like Orwell does it. For 5 hours, you read through text, sort datachunks to their respective profiles, and read unskippable text / call exchanges between the subjects. That is pretty much it. The story is a bit slow and does only gain steam in the last two episodes 4 and 5, but the "gameplay" remains the same.

Perhaps even more annoying is that there is no overall lesson to be learned here; it is very much a self-containing story with no real moral aside from the obvious and ham-fisted "government can see everything you do = bad", which does not even really stick the landing as the game actually shows a few reasons for why the government may want to do such a thing, right or not.

As a game, there is not much here aside from essentially reading a more tedious novel while constantly having to switch between profiles with little choice until the end. As a story, there is some good here, but it is not engaging enough even despite the short length.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] George Orwell rolls in his grave [/h1]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is an interactive novel exploring the increasingly popular notion that G. Orwell’s iconic “1984” ended up being a guideline for running a country, rather than a warning to its citizens. True to dystopian tones of its inspiration, the title opens up with a bombing attack on a public plaza. Several people were killed, perpetrators are unknown and public is in an uproar. This where you come in, as hand-picked investigator you will use the latest marvel of civil protection technology – Orwell, to solve the case. Orwell “the first and the last line of defence against terrorism” is a powerful software capable of accessing everything connected to the internet. Once a person is authorised by higher-ups for investigation, you are to upload any useful chunks of data into the software and Orwell will process them, granting you access to further information on the target. Person of interest has their phone number on their social media page? Now you can listen to their calls. An e-mail address published on their company’s website? Let’s take a peek inside. Is that a PC id number? You know the drill by now.

[b] Big brother stays vigilant [/b]
With power of Orwell at your fingertips, the player becomes breach of privacy incarnate, yet the decision whether to upload something or not is yours to make. At times you will have conflicting data, that may mislead the authorities acting upon your investigation, while certain details can be ignored altogether. On the other hand, there are also key data chunks that have to be uploaded in order to progress the story and, especially at early stages, there are not a lot of choices to make. Orwell is counterintuitive at first and software’s interpretation of data provided is downright puzzling at times. You better adapt to your new role quickly, as at certain junctions your choices will have an impact at the rest of the story.

It might have drawn your attention that I have addressed the title in question as an “interactive novel”, rather than a game. This is primarily due to the fact that aforementioned limited choice of data chunks thrown into the system is as far as gameplay goes. Alas, it is much easier to regard Orwell as a book, with webpages being equivalent of descriptions and eavesdropped calls and chats being the dialogues. Your investigation quickly unveils a hint of deeply-rooted conspiracy being at work and bombing is but a beginning of something much bigger. Plot divided into 5 chapters thickens quickly and while the general direction of the story is set in stone, your choices can greatly alter fate of certain characters and the ending is yours to twist.

[b] Blessed be the mind too small to question [/b]
Orwell is rather straight-forward with its thought-provoking intent. While the title’s plot unveils in delightfully ambiguous “The Nation”, it doesn’t take a particularly big leap of logic to start drawing parallels. Especially with themes of invigilation, media manipulation and a classic question of “whether the ends justify the means”. As with most of such questions and ideas, Orwell will be whatever you choose to make of it. It won’t be long though, as the title takes roughly 5 hours to complete, making it possible to finish Orwell in a single sitting. That said, the story is divided into coherent chapters of similar length, highlighted by the game as a good moment for a break, should you need one. Orwell is commendable for finding multiple sensible ways to underline impending conclusion of a plot thread, while staying reasonable from in-universe perspective.

Another facet of Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, deserving a separate mention is the art style of the game. Admittedly, the opening cutscene fells remarkably clunky but everything past this very beginning is static images, allowing the style to truly shine. Every picture is built from colourful polygons giving the illustrations believable, yet somewhat obscured, feel to it. Much like the setting of the story, the visuals are deliberately vague, leaving making the parallels up to the player. 

When approached as a book, Orwell makes for enjoyable read with a highly unorthodox mode of delivery. I can easily recommend it to every fan of criminal thriller and political fiction as you should find yourself right at home. If one were to approach the title as a game though, there is very little to speak of. Should you also happen to be the type to skip dialogues in games as a habit, you should probably avoid Orwell like a plague.

P.S. Once you exit Orwell, you are greeted by advertisement of a sequel - Orwell: Ignorance is Strength. Fear not though, Keeping an Eye On You provides a complete storyline, no “to be continued” ending attached.

review_text_raw:
--SPOILERS AHEAD--

Orwell is the tale of an idealistic german teacher and privacy crusader, who once thought that Privacy and Security could go hand on hand, linked and managed by the use of a Glorified Ethics Manual.

Like all nice things, of course that was doomed to fail. Not an oversight, a bug, or any kind of mistake on the system. It was humanity itself that doomed the man's dream to fail...or succed. 

In Orwell, you are that "humanity", a virtual avatar of yourself, selected by the Goverment of "The Nation" to operate this impressive machine, and act as judge and jury (but not executioner, mind you), all in the name of Security and Stability. A game where choices matter, and even the most petty things you decide to inform (or ignore) have consequences to people out there, decides their fate, their lives. I have to say that at first I couldn't grasp this concept. My first play was very pro-Goverment, and by the end of it, I felt good: I improved the Nation, I helped people. 

But if you are going to play, play more than once. Try to change your choices, ignore things and highlight others. With repetition, the characters started growing on me. People I saw as assholes at first were suddenly adquiring new traits I never saw or thought before. And with repetition, I saw how Orwell was fucking the lifes of these people, I saw the tragedy of these little self-contained stories. 

+Interesting plot
+Simple and clean visuals add to the overall theme of the game
+It's good to play a Big Brother Simulator

-Too short for my taste. I spaced each episode a day apart to make it last, but you could easily beat it in a day.
-Some...concepts about how Orwell works in Ep.5 are a bit silly. "Abe's" plan doesn't make much sense, while there are plenty of reasons for following Initiate's plan, or even for following Delacroix's orders. 

Score: 8/10. Would play again.

It's borderline but I'd lean towards no.

Effectively choose your own adventure, with the agency being 'what you leave out' by not reporting it to the agency.
The problem is some things are required to be reported to move the plot forward, and those aren't marked in any special way. Thus, there were a few times where I just started reporting everything, even if I wanted to leave it out.

Additionally, the plot anded up being "mass surveillance is bad" (obviously given the title), but by being "reports everything" robot, I caught two mass murderers, and wasted one innocent person's time in jail for a few days. Then I was lectured by a mass murderer and an anti-government hacker for 5 minutes, while waiting for the police to take the murderer away.

Somehow the terrible writing has pushed me more towards being pro surveillance lol.

Finally, it's really short (3hr), but I got it for 6 bucks, so I think I got my money's worth.

Overall like I said really borderline, but I wouldn't recommend it to most people.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]A memorable and engaging experience.[/h1]

Orwell puts you in the shoes of an investigator working for a police state. The goal is to identify and build a case against suspected terrorists using both publicly available and personal/confidential information. Information you upload enables access to further sources. Uploading mention of a notable injury will unlock access to the person's medical records; finding a phone number or email lets you spy in on their correspondence etc. 

But information you upload could be incorrect, or misinterpreted/twisted to suit the government's agenda. How far will you go? Who will you condemn?

[h1]How is it?[/h1]

This core is compelling and unique enough to carry the game through to its conclusion. The comparisons to Papers Please are obvious, but Orwell is far more expansive. Where Papers Please created tension by pitting you against a time limit, Orwell creates a complex, intriguing and politically relevant narrative where you never truly know who is or isn't guilty. It is hard to discuss in detail without spoiling, but the story is full of twists and turns and finds a way to successfully play out dramatic scenes that you experience from behind the safety of your computer screen and the shield of Orwell.

The soundtrack compliments the game nicely, and is used effectively to punctuate important revelations in the story.

It's entirely text-based, and game length depends entirely on your reading speed and habits. Speed-reading and scanning for pertinent information (which the game highlights for you) can shorten the game to 3-4 hours. A more thorough and careful reading, especially if read aloud, can extend your playtime to 8 hours. The game will be a one-time experience for most players, but the game lets you play each episode individually once cleared, and there's enough agency in what optional & conflicting information you upload that replayability is there for those that want it.

[h1]However[/h1]

The game has enough flaws to feel like it wasn't thoroughly tested.

Conflicting information is highlighted in yellow, rather than blue. You can only upload one of these, so the game highlights conflicting information before you've identified what it conflicts with. This is both a minor spoiler and very awkward, and could have easily been handled better.

It's easy to get overwhelmed with information. The game highlights sources with new information for you, but distinguishing between what is optional and mandatory to upload is not obvious. Perhaps this is intentional, but it is too easy to be stuck in a deadlock with 30 possible sources to go through trying to find the one piece of mandatory information you refrained from uploading the first time. An additional icon highlighting old sources with uploadable information would have made this much less tedious.

Spying in on peoples phone conversations happens in real time. This has a wonderful voyeuristic feel to it, but the conversations progress far too fast to read aloud at a comfortable speaking pace. This would be fine if they didn't contain time-sensitive information that needs to be uploaded during the conversation itself. Anyone streaming this or reading aloud to themselves will be caught in the awkward spot of either missing the window to upload information, or have to voice act far too fast for the conversation to sound natural.

Finally, the writing itself is simply poor. I wonder if it was written by a native English speaker or a trained writer. The grammar is awkward, misleading or just incorrect far too often, and this does detract from the otherwise believable world and engaging story the game creates. Simple proof-reading would have solved this.

None of these are game-breaking or significantly ruin the game, but all are so needless, so simply and easily solved that their inclusions are frustrating.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

If you liked Papers Please, find the theme compelling or want a unique text-based game, you'll enjoy this. It comes with too many niggling issues to recommend at full price, but with a small discount this will be a worthwhile experience that will stay with you for years to come.
