review_text_raw:
Overall Rating: 8.5/10

If you've ever read any dystopic novels and enjoyed them (not just 1984, but Brave New World, Fahrenheit 451 etc.) then this is a very fun game to enter such a world. However the perspective change with Orwell is that you become the one controlling the panopticon, and your choices determine who gets arrested and killed, what big events happen in the game, and what ultimately happens to this program that allows 'foreigners' to spy on people of 'The Nation' (the fictional country the game is set in). 

This is also quite a nice game to play if you don't feel up to quick or intense action you find in others. This game, if you want to delve deep into the world, contains a lot of reading and clicking/dragging highlighted bits of text. That's about it. And you can enjoy 5-8 hours of this, which is especially good if you get this game very cheaply when it comes on sale. The story is engaging and has very interesting characters. I have not played the sequel, but reviews on it say that it's not as good as the first Orwell game (this one). 

Pros: 
- very good soundtrack
- good story, but has little replayability considering you already know the truth of what happens later, and the consequences of your choices
- you can replay individual chapters when you go to "Profile Options" after completing the game on a profile, which means it is very easy to achievement hunt (which is what I did)
- good length of the game, even if it's not on sale
- unique mechanics I haven't played in a game before (I don't play all that many indies however)

Cons:
- the story replayability aspect
- if you're not very interested in 1984 or Orwell's writings then this may not interest you all that much considering that this game is one big reference to 1984

review_text_raw:
[h1] ORWELL REVIEW [/h1]


[b] What is Orwell? [/b] 
Orwell is a story-driven puzzle/mystery game in which you, someone outside 'The Nation', take control of Orwell - the latest security system designed to counteract terrorism, etc. Its a game that focuses more on giving you an experience with its story and plot rather than with engaging gameplay. 

[u] STORY [/u] 
Orwell isn't shy in showing its influences from George Orwells '1984' (clearly), and thats a good thing. '1984' is considered by many to be one of the best pieces of literature ever written, and with very good reason - it predicts a horrible shift in society which results in a dystopian state run with an iron fist and constant survelliance and information control on its populace. George Orwell's novel takes place after this dytopian rule has been established for years, so we do not truly understand how it became so all-powerful to begin with, however, Orwell takes a look at what it may be like at the start of this rule, with a brand new system, called ORWELL, being used to solve a terror attack on 'The Nation'. When Orwell wrote '1984' there was no internet, or social media, etc. and this game takes a look at how '1984' would be had those things been considered, and trying to basically update '1984' for a modern audience and make it culturally relevant today is no small feat, and happily, I can say they have done a superb job of capturing, while updating, George Orwell's original vision.  

Overall Story Score = 9/10 (Masterful) 


[u] GAMEPLAY [/u]
Gameplay in Orwell is probably the games weakest point as there's not much actual 'gameplay' involved. For the most part Orwell's gameplay consists of reading text documents, web pages, phonecall logs, emails, etc. and finding relevant text and info and attaching it to certain peoples files. While this may sound completely mundane it is actually quite a refreshing take on detective gameplay and feels like you are genuinely investigating people. Although, personally, towards the climax of the game I found trying to find that one last clue to tie things together quite frustrating and slowed the pace of the game. 

Overall Gameplay Score = 6/10 (Good)


[u] GRAPHICS [/u] 
Orwell uses a rather unique cell-shaded polygon art style, very similar to something you would find in a visual novel, and it compliments the game well. As someone who isnt a huge fan of completely drawn art styles Ifound myself really liking the approach this game took in its art direction. 

Overall Graphics Score = 7/10 (Great) 


[u] SOUND [/u] 
Orwell has a nice relaxing soundtrack for the most part with occasional moments of high intensity. The soundtrack perfectly fits the game and was particularly noticable during certain parts of the game which greatly increased the impact of those moments. Also, the soundtrack doesn't get annoying or repetative at any point which is impressive considering the length of time you are listening to it. Saying all that though, its by no means a memorable soundtrack or anything special. 

Overall Sound Score = 6/10 (Good) 


[u] LASTING APPEAL [/u] 
It took me roughly 4 hours to play through the story once, and I am plannign at some point to play through it once more, but that will probably be the max I play. I personally wouldn't pay full price just purely due to the price-to-playtime ratio but on sale I would definitely pick it up. Overall though the lasting appeal is quite poor due to it being a story driven game all based on a whodunnit payoff, which makes replayability a bit less appealing. There are multiple endings however so if you want to get all of them you may get more out of it than most.

Overall Lasting Appeal Score = 4/10 (Below Average)


[b] OVERALL SCORE = 7/10 - Great [/b]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is an narrative game with unique gameplay. The game puts you in the shoes of an investigator whose job it is to keep the Nation safe. You work with the titular program 'Orwell' which is an advanced search engine that lets you browse the in game internet in search of terrorists. You will start of by reading through public blogs, forums and social media. But as the stakes rise and the public information dries up you will find yourself spending more and more time eavesdropping on phone calls and hacking into personal files.

The feel of the game reminds me a bit of Deus Ex. I personally loved hacking computers and reading emails in those games, and Orwell turns this side activity into a full game. This means that you will do a lot of reading, although the useable pieces of information are always highlighted. You can upload these 'data chunks' to your superior, who will act on the information you feed him. Your superior cannot read anything except for the parts you upload, which gives you the freedom to interpret the data and even 'spin' it. Do you focus on the information that marks someone as potentially dangerous or do you focus on their peaceful side? This will ofcourse have consequences down the road.

Speaking of consequences, these are actually real in this game. Although your actions will not change the core structure of the narrative, they will have a very clear impact. All suspects can be arrested, one can be killed, or you can let them all go free. What makes this game unique is that most consequences are not directly tied to a single choice, but to a whole set of smaller decisions. There is no 'do you let this person live?' moment. Instead the choices you made in what data you upload and what information you ignore will determine the fate of the characters. The ending may appear to be a 'choose your own ending' affair at first, but a replay made it clear to me that your earlier choices will still impact the ending you get.

The theme of the game is privacy vs safety. But unlike other games or media on this subject, there is no clear black or white. The game shows that your work can save lives, but that it also has the potential to ruin them. The characters constantly move between light grey and dark grey, sometimes praising violence and sometimes worrying about their family. Only in the final episode do two characters clearly turn out to be evil, but even then the game takes no position on the core debate, allowing the player the freedom to think about it themselves.

Sadly the game has a very short runtime. The first play through will take about 4-5 hours. If you skip past most text you will be done even faster. The game has some replay value, partially due to its short length, but the first play through is much more fun than the second.

There is one potential problem with this game: it is all in text. If you like reading lore, this will be fine. But if you tend to skip across text, the game will likely become boring fast. Even the phone calls are in text. Only the intro is animated. Despite this, the game can still be nail biting tense as police move in on the potential location of a bomb or terrorist and you can do little but follow the news and related phone calls, hoping that your work was enough to save the day.

Tl;dr: a great narrative game with actual choices, but lots of text. If you skipped to the tl;dr there is probably too much text for you!

The characters constantly move between light grey and dark grey, sometimes praising violence and sometimes worrying about their family. Only in the final episode do two characters clearly turn out to be evil, but even then the game takes no position on the core debate, allowing the player the freedom to think about it themselves. Sadly the game has a very short runtime. The first play through will take about 4-5 hours. If you skip past most text you will be done even faster. The game has some replay value, partially due to its short length, but the first play through is much more fun than the second. There is one potential problem with this game: it is all in text. If you like reading lore, this will be fine. But if you tend to skip across text, the game will likely become boring fast. Even the phone calls are in text. Only the intro is animated. Despite this, the game can still be nail biting tense as police move in on the potential location of a bomb or terrorist and you can do little but follow the news and related phone calls, hoping that your work was enough to save the day. Tl;dr: a great narrative game with actual choices, but lots of text. If you skipped to the tl;dr there is probably too much text for you!

review_text_raw:
The Gameplay:
The style of gameplay is certainly unorthodox from your standard games, but it is easy to understand and even empowering. You essentially link relevant information regarding a person or event and depending on how you do that, certain events will play out.

The Story:
You operate a special hacking suite provided by the government to pry into someone's life and essentially build a report about the person and their activities. There is person receiving your report and they act on what you provide. It was interesting to follow and felt real enough to hit home a lot of times. 

The Visuals:
The art choice was interesting for the characters giving them a somewhat pixelated look. The actual HUD was very nice to look at and easy to use. 

The Sound:
The soundtrack was distinct and set a nice atmosphere for the work you are about to do. Nothing else really stood out save for some of the menu noises which were neat. 


The Experience:
When getting this game, I thought I would find it mildly entertaining. I was not prepared for how into the game I would end up getting. I was so enthralled with the way the investigation pans out that I got a notepad and started jotting down relevant info and dates to make sure I could solve the case. 

It has a decent amount of replayability since you can choose different options which very satisfyingly changes the context of the rest of the story. The game hit that sweet spot of not being too short nor being too long. Overall I feel Orwell did a good job of putting you in the seat of the Investigator and keeping the game and story fresh.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I'll admit, I was skeptical, even with all the glowing reviews on Steam. However, bored with playing the same old games, I decided to give the game a try since it wasn't even 10$. As I started up the game, I asked myself - how this game could possibly keep me interested? It's a game where you're literally staring at a 'computer' screen in-game.. when you're already staring at a computer screen in real life. Not even 10 minutes in and I was hooked. I needed more information and I needed it NOW! I got really invested in the fictional characters stories, lives and background; why did she break up with him? How long were they dating? Why is 'X's relationship with her parents so strained? I looked through every single e-mail and chat message I could find. I listened to countless phone calls and actually cared what was said and listened intently. All the while snickering to myself because the fictional characters didn't know I was listening in on their conversations. 

This game proves that sometimes being innovative and creative pays off. The game was worth every last dollar. It's relatively short (6 hours) and  I played all the episodes straight through, but it still managed to keep me excited and interest throughout the whole game. I kept playing 'just 10 more minutes' to find new information. Although only 6 hours long, I felt like it's the perfect length. Any longer and I probably would have started getting annoyed (because I did want to find out the ending to the story). 

The only issues I had with the game was that it doesn't really explain how the 'upload information' works. It tells you very briefly what your job is - to upload information, but I didn't understand that I could literally choose what information to upload and what to withold. I thought I had to upload certain information to continue with the story - turns out that may not have necessarily been the case. I actually got an ending I didn't intend because even at the end of the game I wasn't really sure what I was supposed to be doing (how did I access information, not upload it but still continue with the story?). You would think 'upload information' would be an easy concept to understand and wouldn't really need a tutorial, but in my case I would have liked a proper 2-3 minute introduction to how Orwell 'works'. The fact that you can choose what you do and do not upload, and depending on that - there will be different concequences. 
The highlighting of relevant text kinda made the game too easy, but I do understand the necessity of the function. Any real-life program such as Orwell would probably have a similar feature that highlights relevant information. I felt like it made the game more realistic because occassionally while reading an on-going chat, I could quickly scan for relevant information that was highlighted - upload it - and then continue reading the conversation. 
I really idn't realize that my actions of uploading certain information would have concequences; I guess I thought the game was a lot more linear, not that I could actually influence what happened by what I did or did not upload. 

This was really unique, both in game-playstyle as well as story telling. I'll be playing it again, that's for sure.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a game where you take control of a operator of a information gathering tool that your government has recently implemented to help collect data on suspects of crimes.You are pared together with another investigator that you submit data that they will use to draw a conclusion. The investigator you are pared with only has the information you submit and cannot see what you are currently browsing thus giving you freedom to determin what conclusion they draw. The game has different outcomes and your actions threwout the game influence future events. If you enjoy mystery games this is a must, if you are skepitical about governmental survailence I recommend this game. It presents a fair perspective on all angles of that argument and is very honest on that regard. I have attempted to keep this spoiler free and hope I have suceeded while giving useful information.
